content:
<Rep. Maxine Waters, Rep. Nydia M. Velázquez, Rep. Stephen F. Lynch, Rep. Al Green, Rep. Joyce Beatty, Rep. Rashida Tlaib, Rep. Sylvia R. Garcia>: H.R. 5262 amends several banking laws to completely waive a review related to competition for proposed mergers that would result in a bank under $10 billion in assets, regardless of whether the bank would become the only lender in a particular community and lead to higher financing charges. The bill also includes an annual adjustment calculation based on nominal GDP that does not account for inflation, which could quickly increase the threshold. These sweeping reforms do nothing to improve a review process already widely criticized as a rubber-stamp exercise and will accelerate consolidation and lead to fewer community banks.
Community banks and credit unions play a key role in providing financial access to communities throughout the country.\1\ There has been a steady, decades-long consolidation trend dating back to the 1980s, when restrictions relating to banks' multiple branches and across state lines were relaxed. In 1984, there were nearly 15,000 commercial banks and 15,000 credit unions, more than two-thirds of which have since disappeared, many through mergers.\2\ Meanwhile, there has been a reduction in bank branches throughout many communities, leaving certain communities in ``banking deserts'' where there may not be a branch within a 10-mile radius. U.S. bank branches fell from a peak of 82,965 in 2012 to less than 70,000 in 2023, with the largest banks closing at least 3,600 branches during this period.\3\ The Federal Reserve Bank of New York found that low-income census tracts were more than twice as likely to be located in banking deserts than higher income tracts.\4\
\1\CRS, Introduction to Financial Services: Banking (Jan. 13, 2025), and CRS, Introduction to Bank Regulation: Credit Unions and Community Banks: A Comparison (Dec. 14, 2018).
\2\FDIC, BankFind Suite--Annual Historical Bank Data (accessed Apr. 27, 2024); NCUA, Annual Report 1984 (1984); and FSC hearing, Revamping and Revitalizing Banking in the 21st Century (Feb. 8, 2023).
\3\FDIC, BankFind Suite: Find Annual Historical Bank Data (Accessed Feb. 1, 2025); also see Memo for Committee hearing entitled, Holding Megabanks Accountable: An Update on Banking Practices, Programs, and Policies (May 27, 2021).
\4\Federal Reserve Bank of New York, Banking Deserts, Branch Closings, and Soft Information (Mar. 7, 2016).
Democrats and experts have raised concerns that banking regulators have largely rubber-stamped merger applications for many years.\5\ These experts cite to overwhelming approval rates for mergers; for example, the Fed indicated that between 2006 and 2017, it approved 3,316 merger applications, and while other applications were withdrawn, the agency formally denied zero applications during that time.\6\ Even when accounting for withdrawn applications, the approval rate has been extremely high; in 2021 and 2022, the Fed approved roughly 97% and 94% of M&A applications, respectively, which includes withdrawn applications.\7\
\5\See FSC, Ranking Member Waters Leads 15 Committee Democrats in Urging Banking Regulators to Quickly Revamp Bank Merger Review Procedures Following Proposed Capital One Merger with Discover (Feb. 28, 2024); Jeremy Kress, Modernizing Bank Merger Review, Yale Journal on Regulation (Aug. 17, 2021); Comment Letter from Jeremy Kress to FDIC regarding comments on FDIC Policy on Bank Merger Transactions (May. 31, 2022); and Better Markets, Bank Mergers Require Robust Scrutiny to Ensure that Consumers' Interests Are Not Sacrificed for Wall Street's Profits (May 12, 2025).
\6\See Sen. Elizabeth Warren, Letter from Fed Chair Powell to Sen. Warren (May 10, 2018).
\7\Fed, Banking Applications Activity Semiannual Report, July- December 2023 (Apr. 2024). Also see Fed, Semiannual Reports on Banking Applications Activity (accessed Apr. 27, 2024).
Market consolidation poses risks to consumers and entrepreneurs. Wells Fargo, for example, grew quickly through multiple mergers and eventually became too big to manage,\8\ repeatedly breaking the law by defrauding millions of consumers.\9\ In addition, after the credit card issuer market consolidated between 1994 and 2002, the largest issuers charged consumers higher interest rates compared to smaller issuers, resulting in many consumers paying $400 to $500 more every year in additional financing costs for effectively the same service.\10\ This is partly why Ranking Member Waters and others raised concerns about the merger between Capital One and Discover,\11\ yet even faced with these concerns Trump's regulators approved the merger to create one of the largest U.S. banks and the largest credit card issuer.\12\
\8\FSC, Waters to Wells Fargo: You Are Simply Too Big to Manage (Mar. 12, 2019). Also see OCC, Former Acting Comptroller of the Currency Michael J. Hsu Remarks at Brookings, ``Detecting, Preventing, and Addressing Too Big To Manage,'' (Jan. 17, 2023).
\9\FSC, In Advance of Wells Fargo Hearings, Waters and Green Release Investigative Report Exposing Failures of Megabank's Management, Board, and Regulators (Mar. 4, 2020).
\10\CFPB, The Consumer Credit Card Market (Oct. 25, 2023); CFPB, CFPB Report Finds Large Banks Charge Higher Credit Card Interest Rates than Small Banks and Credit Unions (Feb. 16, 2024); and CFPB, Data spotlight--Credit card data: Small issuers offer lower rates (Feb. 16, 2024).
\11\FSC, Waters Testifies Against Proposed Capital One-Discover Merger at Regulators' Public Meeting (Jul. 19, 2024).
\12\FSC, Ranking Member Maxine Waters Slams Trump Administration's Approval of Capital One-Discover Merger (Apr. 21, 2025).
During debate on H.R. 5262, Republicans rejected an amendment by Ranking Member Waters that would simply require mergers resulting in a bank with more than $100 billion in assets to: have at least one public hearing; have a community benefits plan; and minimize banking deserts related to any branch closures.
Furthermore, while the FDIC, OCC, and Department of Justice under the Biden Administration adopted reforms to strengthen bank merger reviews last year, Trump's regulators have rolled back these reforms.\13\ H.R. 5262 would remove common sense guardrails and would make rubber-stamp merger approvals even more likely. A longstanding aspect of bank merger reviews has been considering competitive factors, such as whether the merged entity would have monopoly power or anti-competitive effects on the business of banking in any part of the country, or whether the public interest in the second factor outweighs any adverse effects on competition.\14\
\13\Consumer Finance Monitor, FDIC proposing rescinding merger policy adopted in September (Mar. 10, 2025).
\14\12 U.S.C. Sec. 1842(c).
Given that roughly 98% of banks have less than $10 billion,\15\ this sweeping reform would effectively waive a critical component of most bank merger reviews. While the sweeping nature of the reform is concerning, it is also unclear what data may justify such a threshold utilized for such a reform. Moreover, the bill contains an unusual annual threshold increase based on nominal GDP growth, which excludes the impact of inflation. This could quickly increase the threshold, exempting more banks from this critical review. For example, nominal GDP grew by nearly 50% from 2018 to today, but only by 18% when using real GDP when accounting for inflation.\16\
\15\See data referenced from FDIC above.
\16\BEA, Gross Domestic Product (accessed Sep. 14, 2025).
All Committee Democrats voted against H.R. 5262 during the markup. H.R. 5262 is also opposed by Americans for Financial Reform, Public Citizen, and Rise Economy. The reforms in H.R. 5262 would likely accelerate consolidation trends for smaller banks and would do nothing to fix a broken merger review process that has allowed megabanks to consolidate market power while ripping off consumers for years.
For these reasons, we oppose H.R. 5262.
Sincerely,
Maxine Waters,
Ranking Member.
Nydia M. Velazquez,
Stephen F. Lynch,
Al Green,
Joyce Beatty,
Rashida Tlaib,
Sylvia R. Garcia,
Members of Congress.
